content: 1. When there is a risk of exposure to blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions, such as during coughing or sneezing, it is essential to use eye protection to prevent contact with sprays of these substances. 2. Gowns should be worn to protect the skin and prevent contamination of clothing during activities that may generate splashes or sprays of blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions. 3. Select a gown appropriate for the activity and the anticipated amount of fluid exposure. If the gown is not fluid-resistant, wear a waterproof apron over it when splashing or spraying of potentially infectious material is expected. 4. Remove soiled gowns as soon as possible, dispose of them in a waste or laundry receptacle as appropriate, and perform hand hygiene immediately afterward. 5. Respiratory hygiene is critical to controlling the spread of pathogens from infected patients to unprotected individuals. This includes applying respiratory hygiene measures for all individuals with respiratory symptoms, especially for diseases transmitted via large droplets or droplet nuclei. 6. Viruses and bacteria causing acute respiratory infections (ARIs) can survive on surfaces for varying periods. Cleaning reduces the bioburden of microorganisms, and disinfection inactivates infectious agents using standard hospital disinfectants. 7. Environmental cleaning and disinfection aim to remove or significantly reduce pathogens on contaminated surfaces and items, breaking the chain of transmission. Disinfection should follow cleaning and be performed using physical or chemical methods to kill microorganisms, excluding spores. 8. Surfaces and equipment that do not come into direct contact with patients do not require disinfection but should be thoroughly cleaned between patient uses. 9. Cleaning patient-care environments should focus on horizontal surfaces, especially those frequently touched or near the patient, and should be performed regularly and upon patient discharge. 10. To avoid aerosol generation of ARI pathogens, use damp cleaning methods (e.g., moistened cloths) rather than dry dusting or sweeping. Cleaning solutions and equipment should be changed frequently to prevent contamination. 11. Equipment used for cleaning and disinfection must be cleaned and dried after each use. Mop heads should be laundered daily and dried thoroughly before storage or reuse. 12. Keep areas around the patient free of unnecessary supplies and equipment to facilitate daily cleaning. Disinfect surfaces used by patients known or suspected to be infected with ARIs of concern. 13. Avoid practices like fogging rooms with disinfectants, as they are potentially dangerous and lack proven disease-control benefits. 14. To reduce aerosol generation during vacuuming, use uncarpeted rooms or areas for patients when possible. If vacuuming is necessary, use a vacuum cleaner equipped with a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter. 15. Reusable patient-care equipment should be cleaned and disinfected according to general protocols before reuse. Equipment used in isolation rooms should be disinfected with approved hospital disinfectants before removal. 16. Reusable respiratory equipment must be properly cleaned and disinfected to ensure safety in ARI patient care. 17. Reusable dishes and eating utensils should be washed in a dishwasher when available. If not, wash them by hand using detergents while wearing non-sterile rubber gloves. Wash these items after each use. 18. Disposable items should be discarded as waste, classified according to relevant state, territory, or national regulations. 19. Contaminated linen should be handled minimally to avoid contamination of air, surfaces, and people. Heavily soiled linen should have solid waste removed (e.g., feces) before being placed in a laundry bag. Avoid sorting linen in patient-care areas. 20. Wash and dry linen according to routine healthcare facility standards. For hot-water laundry cycles, use detergent or disinfectant in water at 70°C (160°F) for at least 25 minutes. For lower temperatures, use appropriate chemicals at proper concentrations. 21. Waste disposal must be safe for handlers and the environment. Waste from ARI-infected patients classified as infectious should be treated and disposed of according to healthcare facility policies and national regulations. 22. Ensure healthcare workers use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) when there is a risk of splash or spray during waste handling. 23. Used equipment, soiled linen, and waste from isolation areas should be placed directly into containers or bags in the isolation room. These should be contained to prevent opening or bursting during transport. Double-bagging is unnecessary if contamination of the bag's exterior is avoided. 24. Personnel handling used equipment, soiled linen, and waste must follow standard precautions and perform hand hygiene after removing PPE. 25. Prevent injuries when using needles, scalpels, and other sharp instruments. Avoid recapping used needles, directing the needle point toward the body, or manually removing needles from disposable syringes. Dispose of sharps in puncture-resistant containers located close to the area of use. 26. Respiratory pathogens transmitted via large droplets include adenovirus, avian influenza A (H5N1), human influenza, and SARS-CoV. During an influenza pandemic, droplet precautions should be applied in addition to standard precautions. 27. Use a medical mask when working within 1 meter of the patient. For practical purposes, it is advisable to wear a mask when entering the patient’s room. 28. Place patients in single rooms or cohort those with the same etiological diagnosis. If this is not possible, group patients with similar clinical diagnoses and epidemiological risk factors, maintaining at least 1 meter of spatial separation. 29. Limit patient movement and ensure they wear medical masks when outside their rooms. 30. Contact transmission of respiratory pathogens can occur through hand contamination and self-inoculation into mucosal surfaces. Contact precautions include PPE, equipment use, environmental measures, and patient placement and transport. 31. Wear clean, non-sterile gloves and gowns when entering the room of a patient under contact precautions. Remove PPE upon leaving and perform hand hygiene. 32. Use disposable or dedicated equipment for patients under contact precautions. If equipment must be shared, clean and disinfect it between uses. 33. Avoid touching the eyes, nose, or mouth with potentially contaminated hands, whether gloved or ungloved. 34. Use single rooms or cohort patients with the same diagnosis to facilitate infection prevention and control measures. Limit patient movement and minimize contact with uninfected individuals. 35. For airborne pathogens, supplement standard precautions with additional measures, such as using a particulate respirator (e.g., N95) when entering isolation rooms or providing care to patients with airborne infectious diseases. 36. Place patients in airborne precaution rooms or well-ventilated separate rooms if isolation rooms are unavailable. Cohort patients with the same diagnosis in well-ventilated areas if single rooms are not available. 37. Perform aerosol-generating procedures in airborne precaution rooms using appropriate PPE. 38. Limit patient movement and ensure they wear medical masks when outside their rooms.
